author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are preparing for a historic trilateral meeting in China.
The leaders of three of the world's biggest nuclear powers are coming together at a critical moment for global security.
The last remaining nuclear arms control treaty between Washington and Moscow expired in February, and Trump has rejected Russia's proposal to extend its limits.
Now he wants China brought into a new agreement, arguing that meaningful arms control is impossible without Beijing.
But China has refused to join negotiations, pointing to the vast disparity between its nuclear arsenal and those of the US and Russia.
So can the three leaders reach a new deal? Or is the world heading towards a new nuclear arms race without any binding limits?

PRESENTER: Alex Marquardt

GUESTS:
Jonathan Fritz: Former US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for East Asia

author: Al Jazeera English
description: Oil pollution from damaged vessels during the war involving Iran is threatening marine ecosystems and coastal communities around the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. The International Maritime Organization had recorded 136 confirmed maritime incidents across the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East region as of November 11, while Greenpeace says satellite monitoring has detected more than 500 oil slicks across the Gulf, the strait and the Arabian Sea since the conflict began. Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace Middle East and North Africa, warns that the pollution threatens protected areas and vulnerable species, including dugongs, turtles and the rare Arabian Sea humpback whale. She says the Gulf's shallow, semi-enclosed waters mean oil pollution can remain in the marine environment for extended periods. Nakat also describes a recently detected slick covering about 300 square kilometres, with a 70-kilometre section appearing thick and dark, indicating heavy oil. Al Jaz
title: Greenpeace warns oil spills could cause lasting damage to Gulf ecosystems

description: Al Jazeera Latin America editor Lucia Newman reflects on 20 years with the network, recalling the challenges of joining a new broadcaster and the opportunity to bring deeper coverage of the region to international audiences. During her career, she has reported on natural disasters, humanitarian crises and mass migration, including the devastating earthquake in Haiti, a deadly mudslide in Colombia’s Amazon region and the dangerous journey of Venezuelan migrants through the Darién Gap. She says the stories that have affected her most are the forced disappearances of hundreds of thousands of people in Mexico, and the lasting anguish of families still searching for their loved ones. Newman also remembers stories of hope, particularly the rescue of 33 Chilean miners who were trapped underground for more than 69 days, which Al Jazeera followed from the early stages of the operation. She also remembers coming face to face with ISIL fighters in Syria, travelling to the Taliban’s heartland in Afghanistan and covering the devastating 2020 Beirut port explosion, an event that affected journalists and residents alike. Among the stories that remain with her is that of Mustafa, an eight-year-old boy who survived an Israeli strike but lost his parents, siblings and other relatives. author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Al Jazeera English senior presenter and correspondent Imran Khan reflects on his two-decade journey with the network, from joining its Doha newsroom when the headquarters was still under construction to reporting from conflict zones and major events around the world. His connection with Al Jazeera began in 2003, when he was a freelance journalist embedded with British forces during the invasion of Iraq. He recalls watching Al Jazeera Arabic challenge reports that Basra had fallen to British forces, an example of the fearless journalism that inspired him to join the network. After becoming a correspondent, he reported from Pakistan, Iran, Syria, Ukraine and other parts of the world, covering conflict and injustice. He also reflects on the dangers faced by journalists and the loss of friends and colleagues in war zones. Now a senior presenter, Khan says he values the opportunity to bring together stories from across the world and remains proud to report under the Al Jazeera name.
